name: Tangil Khondaker
text: Abstract. Backpropagation trains nearly all modern neural networks but requires a fully differentiable computation graph and an activation tape whose memory footprint grows with depth. We study a local, three-factor Hebbian update rule that needs neither, and show it is a provably unbiased estimator of the true loss gradient — so its only failure mode is variance, governed by a measured scaling law, M*·K ≳ S: the probe budget times the feedback bandwidth must cover the loss's coupling scope. We test this directly via a Jacobian coupling-density audit: a Mamba-3-style selective state-space block measures as fully entangled (density 0.874, indistinguishable from self-attention), closing that branch, while a blurring-diffusion denoiser built as a per-mode spectral gain bank measures as exactly diagonal (density 0.000), confirming an existing proof empirically. A follow-up probe-budget experiment confirms the law's second lever — per-channel feedback reaches a fixed alignment target with 5× fewer samples than a global scalar — but even at this optimum the rule costs ≈6.7× backpropagation's FLOPs on an ordinary task. We position this program's value accordingly: not as a blanket efficiency win, but where backpropagation is structurally unavailable or FLOPs are not the binding constraint.
